messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert was seventy-four, a widower, and had spent much of his adult life in roles that demanded steadiness under pressure, including years as a combat pilot. He came to treatment only after several months in which his symptoms had become harder to hide from the people around him. In the course of the intake, he spoke in a controlled, measured way, but there were moments when his face tightened and his jaw set as if he were working hard not to show what he felt. He described a history he had rarely spoken about: in a relationship years earlier, he had been physically abused by a romantic partner, an experience he had kept largely to himself and carried in silence.

He recalled that the abuse was not an isolated incident but something that left him wary of ordinary contact and of the person involved. At times, the smallest physical touch would make him stiffen before he could stop himself. Even now, unexpected touch could bring an immediate jolt through his body, as though he were bracing for harm. He was also unsettled by seeing the offender, and for a long time after the relationship ended he went out of his way to avoid any chance of running into that person or being in places where the encounter might happen. Alcohol smell was another potent reminder for him. He associated it with the atmosphere surrounding the abuse, and if he caught the scent on someone’s breath or in a room, he would feel abruptly on edge, pulled back into the same sense of alarm he had felt then.

Robert spoke about how, over time, he had organized much of his life around not having to face reminders of what happened. He said he had come to believe that he must never allow himself to feel or express anger. When irritation rose in him, he pushed it down immediately, keeping his voice calm and his expression blank. He described this not as a choice that felt natural, but as something he had learned to do because anger felt dangerous and he did not trust what might happen if he let it show. He also avoided anything that reminded him of the person who harmed him, including situations, conversations, and even certain social settings where the memory felt too close. Intimacy was especially difficult. Being emotionally close to others, or allowing himself to depend on someone, felt to him like opening a door he could not close again. After his wife died, this reluctance became even more visible in his daily life, as opportunities for companionship arose but he kept his distance, telling himself that it was safer not to get too close.

In recent months, his threat awareness had become harder to set aside. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert. He would lie awake listening to the house and checking the time, convinced he needed to remain watchful rather than let himself drift off too quickly. During the day he found himself superalert, scanning people and surroundings more than he used to, noticing doors, movements, and the mood of a room almost automatically. He was aware that this left him exhausted, but he also felt that staying on guard was necessary. When something reminded him of the stressful experience, his body reacted strongly. A touch on the arm, the smell of alcohol, or an unexpected glimpse of the offender could bring a rush of physical tension that he experienced as immediate and intense, as though his body knew before his mind did that something was wrong.

These reactions were not confined to abstract memories; they reached into the routines of his current life. In the settings where he now spent his time, he sometimes found himself choosing where to sit, how to position his chair, and how quickly to leave a conversation so he would not be trapped by a reminder. He noticed that he was more guarded with friends and family, and that his efforts to keep anger buried and maintain distance had made him seem more closed off. He did not describe this with regret so much as resignation, as if he had long accepted that this was the price of staying safe.

He sought help now because the symptoms had become impossible to manage alone and because he was tired of living as if any moment could turn threatening. What he most feared was losing control of his vigilance and being caught off guard, especially at night or in situations where he might be touched or unexpectedly reminded of the person who hurt him. At the same time, he said he hoped for a way to sleep without having to stay on alert and to feel less ruled by the need to keep everyone at a distance.
